concept.technique_name: Nikhilam Base Method (Multiplication Near a Base)

examples.problem_statement: Multiply 9996 × 9994

solution.description: Both 9996 and 9994 sit just under 10000, the nearest power of ten, so 10000 is taken as the base for the whole calculation. The four zeros in the base will also fix how wide the right-hand part of the answer must be.
Measure how far each number falls short of the base using All from 9, Last from 10: 9996 is 4 below and 9994 is 6 below. Both numbers are under the base, so both deviations are negative.

solution.operation: Calculate the left part (LHS) of the answer
solution.description: Cross-add: add each number to the other number's deviation. 9996 plus negative 6 and 9994 plus negative 4 both give 9990, and the fact that the two routes agree is the method's built-in check. This 9990 is the left-hand part of the answer.

solution.operation: Calculate the right part (RHS) of the answer
solution.description: Multiply the two deviations to build the right-hand part. Negative 4 times negative 6 is positive 24, since a negative times a negative is positive.

solution.operation: Pad the right part to match base digits
solution.description: The base 10000 has four zeros, so the right-hand part must occupy exactly four digit places. Pad 24 with two leading zeros to write it as 0024.

solution.operation: Combine LHS and RHS for the final answer
solution.description: Write the left-hand part and the padded right-hand part side by side, so 9990 followed by 0024 reads as the product 99900024.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: The Vedic method scores over the traditional method in terms of speed and simplicity by a huge margin.'}
{'point': 'Note: You are well equipped with three different methods: Traditional, Criss-Cross, and Base Method.'}
{'point': 'Tip: If the number is closer to any of the bases or their sub-multiples, use the Base Method.'}
{'point': 'If it is not close to any such number, use the Criss-Cross system.'}
{'point': 'Caution: When RHS exceeds the number of zeros in the base, carry over appropriately.'}
common_mistakes: Writing the right-hand part as 24 instead of 0024, which shortens the answer to 990024 - the base 10000 has four zeros, so the right part needs four digit places.
Treating the product of the two deviations as negative; negative 4 times negative 6 is positive 24, not minus 24.
Cross-adding the wrong pair, such as 9996 plus its own deviation of negative 4, instead of adding each number to the other number's deviation.

concept.sub_category: Yavadunam (Whatever the Extent of its Deficiency)

examples.problem_statement: (Q) Find the square of 8

solution.description: The nearest power of ten to 8 is 10, so 10 becomes the base. Its single zero will later fix the right-hand part of the answer at one digit.

solution.operation: Find the deficiency from the base
solution.description: Measure the shortfall from the base: 10 minus 8 leaves a deficiency of 2. Everything else in Yavadunam is built from this one number.

solution.operation: Subtract the deficiency from the number to get left part
solution.description: Yavadunam says to reduce the number by its own deficiency, so 8 minus 2 gives 6. This is the left-hand part of the answer.

solution.operation: Square the deficiency to get right part
solution.description: Square that same deficiency to build the right-hand part: 2 squared is 4.
Place the left part in the tens position and the right part in the units position, so 6 times 10 plus 4 gives 64, the square of 8.

examples.problem_statement: (Q) Find the square of 96

solution.operation: Take nearest power of 10 as base (100)
solution.description: 96 lies just under 100, so 100 is the base. Its two zeros mean the right-hand part will have to fill two digit places.
96 falls 4 short of 100, so reduce 96 by that deficiency of 4 to get 92 as the left-hand part.
Square the deficiency to get the right-hand part: 4 squared is 16, which already occupies the two digit places the base allows.
Write the left part followed by the right part, so 92 and 16 combine to read 9216 as the square of 96.

examples.problem_statement: (Q) Find the square of 988

solution.operation: Take nearest power of 10 as base (1000)
solution.description: 988 is nearest to 1000, so 1000 is the base here. Its three zeros mean the right-hand part must fill three digit places.
The shortfall is 1000 minus 988, which is 12. Subtracting that deficiency from 988 gives 976 as the left-hand part.
Square the deficiency for the right-hand part: 12 squared is 144, which happens to fill all three digit places exactly.
Join the two parts, 976 then 144, to read the square of 988 as 976144.

examples.problem_statement: (Q) Find the square of 97

solution.operation: Take nearest power of 10 as base (100)
solution.description: 97 is nearest to 100, so 100 is the base. Two zeros in the base means the right-hand part needs two digit places.
97 is 3 short of the base, so subtract that deficiency from 97 to get 94 as the left-hand part.

solution.operation: Square the deficiency (3² = 09) — padded with leading zero for 2-digit RHS
solution.description: Square the deficiency: 3 squared is 9, a single digit. Because the base allows two digit places on the right, it is written as 09 rather than 9.
Place 94 before the padded 09 so the square of 97 reads 9409 rather than the wrong 949.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: The Yavadunam rule applies to squaring numbers near a power of ten.'}
{'point': 'For bases with multiple zeros (e.g., 100, 1000), ensure the RHS matches the number of digits in the base by padding with leading zeros if necessary.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Do not forget to square the deficiency — this is the second critical part of the rule.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Practice identifying the nearest power of ten quickly and mentally calculate the deficiency subtraction and squaring steps consecutively.'}
common_mistakes: Writing the squared deficiency of 97 as 9 instead of 09, which collapses the answer to 949 instead of 9409.
Subtracting the deficiency from the base instead of from the number, for example computing 1000 minus 12 rather than 988 minus 12 for the left-hand part.
Squaring the number's last digit instead of its deficiency, which happens to look right for 96 but fails immediately for 988.

examples.problem_statement: (Q) What is the product of 9993 multiplied by 9997.

solution.description: Both 9993 and 9997 sit just under 10000, so 10000 is taken as the base and each number is written as the base minus a small shortfall: 7 for the first and 3 for the second.

solution.operation: Apply the formula for multiplication near a base
solution.result: a \times b = (base + d_1) \times (base + d_2) = base \times (base + d_1 + d_2) + (d_1 \times d_2)
solution.description: State the base rule in general form before putting numbers in it: the product equals the base times the quantity base plus both deviations, plus the product of the two deviations. Here the base is 10000 and the deviations are negative 7 and negative 3.
Work the first part of that rule. The base plus the two deviations gives 9990, and multiplying by the base 10000 gives 99900000, which is the left portion already shifted into its place value.
Work the second part: multiply the two deviations together. Negative 7 times negative 3 is positive 21.
Add the two parts, 99900000 plus 21, to get the product 99900021.

Check the result with digit-sums rather than by remultiplying. 9993 reduces to 3 and 9997 reduces to 7; 3 times 7 is 21, which reduces to 3, and the product 99900021 also reduces to 3. The agreement is consistent with the answer being correct.

solution.operation: Calculate digit sum of cube root
solution.description: Reduce the cube root to a single digit before doing anything else: 13 has digits adding to 4, so 4 is the stand-in for 13 in this check.
Apply the same operation to the stand-in that the claim applies to the number itself. The claim is about a cube, so cube the stand-in: 4 cubed is 64.
Reduce that outcome to a single digit: 64 gives 6 plus 4, which is 10, and 10 reduces to 1. Any genuine cube of 13 must have digit-sum 1.

solution.operation: Compare with digit sum of cube
solution.description: Reduce the number under test the same way: 2197 gives 19, then 10, then 1. The two single digits match, so 2197 is consistent with being the cube of 13.

concept.technique_name: Magic Square Construction by South-East Movement

examples.problem_statement: How are magic squares formed? Construct a magic square using the following rules: (1) Always put the number $1$ in the centre-most square of the last column. (2) After inserting a number in a square move to the square in the south-east direction and fill it with the next number. (3) If the square in the south-east direction cannot be filled, then move to the square in the west and fill it with the next number. (4) When you have filled a number in the last square of the grid, fill the next number in the square to its west. solution.operation: Construct 3x3 magic square using given rules
solution.description: Build the 3 by 3 grid by following the stated rules: put 1 in the centre-most square of the last column, then step south-east for each next number, wrapping around to the opposite side when the step leaves the grid and moving west when the south-east square is unavailable. The completed grid reads 4, 3, 8 across the top, 9, 5, 1 in the middle, and 2, 7, 6 along the bottom.
Test the construction row by row. Each of the three rows totals 15, so the horizontal condition of a magic square is met.
Test the same grid down its columns. Each column also totals 15, so the vertical condition holds as well.
Finally test the two diagonals: 4, 5 and 6 total 15, and 8, 5 and 2 total 15. With rows, columns and diagonals all equal, the grid is confirmed as a magic square.

solution.operation: Construct 5x5 magic square using same rules
